cse-2026-1-cs-4.approach: Ask, for each mode, where the operand comes from and what the address arithmetic looks like; the high-level construct that compiles to that arithmetic is the match. Immediate = value inside the instruction, indirect = follow a stored address, base+index = start + i, base+fixed displacement = start + field offset.

steps.title: Immediate → constant
steps.body: In immediate mode the operand itself is a field of the instruction, e.g. `ADD R1, #5`. It is fixed when the program is compiled, so it can only hold a **constant** (literal) of the program: **P–4**.

steps.title: Indirect → pointer
steps.body: In indirect mode the instruction names a location that holds the **address** of the operand: $EA = M[A]$ (or $EA = R$ for register indirect). A variable that stores an address and is dereferenced is exactly a **pointer** (`*p`): **Q–2**.

steps.title: Base with index → array element
steps.body: Here $EA = \text{base} + \text{index register}$. The base holds the start of an array and the index register holds the run-time subscript (scaled by element size), so `A[i]` compiles to this mode: **R–1**.

steps.title: Base with displacement → record field
steps.body:
Here $EA = \text{base} + d$ with $d$ a **constant** in the instruction. A base register pointing to a record (struct) plus the fixed, compile-time offset of a field gives `r.field`: **S–3**.

So the matching is **P–4, Q–2, R–1, S–3**, which is option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: Gets P and R right but swaps Q and S: an indirect operand is a stored address (pointer), while a fixed displacement from a base selects a record field, not a pointer.
Immediate–constant, indirect–pointer, base+index–array element, base+displacement–record field: every pair matches the effective-address arithmetic.
An immediate value is fixed in the instruction, so it cannot be an array element that varies at run time; indirect is not a constant either.
Immediate cannot hold a pointer target (that is indirect), and a constant needs no address calculation, so S–4 is wrong.

cse-2026-1-cs-4.shortcut: Variable offset (index register) ⇒ array; constant offset (displacement) ⇒ record field; address stored in memory ⇒ pointer; value in the instruction ⇒ constant. Only (B) has P–4 and Q–2 together.
pitfalls: Confusing "base with index" and "base with displacement": the index is a run-time register (array subscript), the displacement is a compile-time constant (field offset).
Matching indirect with a record because records are "accessed through a base".
cse-2026-1-cs-4.verification: Compile `x = A[i] + r.f + *p + 5` mentally: `A[i]` → `LOAD R, (Rb + Ri)`, `r.f` → `LOAD R, d(Rb)`, `*p` → `LOAD R, @p`, `5` → `#5` — exactly the pairs in (B).

cse-2026-1-cs-5.approach: Use the defining rule of a load-store ISA: only LOAD and STORE may touch memory; every ALU instruction (ADD) must take all its operands from registers. Reject every option whose ADD names a memory operand.

steps.title: What load-store means
steps.body: In a load-store architecture memory is accessed **only** by `LOAD` (memory → register) and `STORE` (register → memory). ALU instructions such as `ADD` are register–register: destination and both sources must be registers. Here X, Y, Z are memory operands and R0–R2 are registers.

steps.title: Check every ADD for memory operands
steps.body:
- (A) `ADD Z, X, Y` — all three operands are in memory. ✗
- (B) `ADD Z, R0, Y` — destination Z and source Y are memory. ✗
- (C) `ADD R0, X, Y` — both sources X and Y are memory. ✗
- (D) `ADD R2, R0, R1` — all registers. ✓

steps.title: Trace the valid sequence
steps.body:
Option (D):

1. `LOAD R0, X` — $R0 \leftarrow X$
2. `LOAD R1, Y` — $R1 \leftarrow Y$
3. `ADD R2, R0, R1` — $R2 \leftarrow R0 + R1 = X + Y$ (first operand is the destination)
4. `STORE Z, R2` — $Z \leftarrow R2$

So $Z = X + Y$ and every memory access is a LOAD or STORE.

answer.value: `LOAD R0, X; LOAD R1, Y; ADD R2, R0, R1; STORE Z, R2` — option (D)

optionAnalysis.reason: A memory-to-memory (three-address CISC style) ADD; a load-store ISA has no ALU instruction with memory operands.
Loads X correctly, but `ADD Z, R0, Y` still reads Y from memory and writes Z to memory inside an ALU instruction.
Stores through a register correctly, but `ADD R0, X, Y` reads both sources directly from memory.
Two LOADs, a register–register ADD and a STORE: the only sequence that respects the load-store rule and computes Z = X + Y.

cse-2026-1-cs-5.shortcut: In a load-store ISA every ADD must look like `ADD Rd, Rs, Rt`. Only (D) has such an ADD.
pitfalls: Picking the shortest sequence (A) — that is a memory-memory architecture.
Thinking one LOAD is enough (B): Y and Z are still memory operands of ADD.
cse-2026-1-cs-5.verification: Count memory accesses: (D) has exactly three (two loads, one store), the minimum for reading two memory operands and writing one — any shorter sequence must let an ALU instruction touch memory.

cse-2026-1-cs-6.approach: A data hazard arises when a later instruction needs a register value that an earlier instruction has not yet written back — a true (flow) dependence, i.e. read-after-write. Check which dependence type involves a value actually flowing between instructions.

steps.title: Read-after-write is a true dependence
steps.body: Example: `I1: ADD R1, R2, R3` then `I2: SUB R4, R1, R5`. In a 5-stage pipeline I1 writes R1 in WB (cycle 5) but I2 reads R1 in ID (cycle 3) — two cycles too early. Without forwarding or stalls I2 reads the stale R1: a **data hazard (RAW)**.

steps.title: Read-after-read never conflicts
steps.body: Two instructions only **reading** the same register cannot interfere — no value is produced, so no ordering constraint exists. RAR is not a dependence at all.

steps.title: WAR and WAW in a classic pipeline
steps.body: WAR (anti) and WAW (output) are only **name** dependences. In the standard in-order pipeline every instruction reads registers in ID and writes in WB, in program order, so a later write can never overtake an earlier read or write — they cause no hazard there (they matter only with out-of-order completion, and register renaming removes them). The dependence that **causes** data hazards is **read-after-write**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Reading a register twice creates no dependence: neither instruction changes the value.
A true (flow) dependence: the consumer may read the register before the producer writes it back — the classic data hazard, fixed by forwarding or stalling.
An anti-dependence; in the in-order pipeline reads (ID) always happen before later writes (WB), so it cannot cause a hazard there.
An output dependence; writes complete in program order in the in-order pipeline, so the final value is always correct.

cse-2026-1-cs-6.shortcut: Only a value flowing from producer to consumer (RAW) is a hazard in the basic pipeline; RAR is never a hazard.
pitfalls: Choosing WAR/WAW because they are called "hazards" in out-of-order (Tomasulo/scoreboard) designs — the question is about a pipelined processor in general, where RAW is the data hazard.
Thinking RAR needs ordering.
cse-2026-1-cs-6.verification: The forwarding path in the diagram (EX of I1 → EX of I2) exists only because of RAW; no hardware is ever added for RAR.

animation.title: RAW on R1: I1 = ADD R1,R2,R3; I2 = SUB R4,R1,R5
animation.caption: I2 reads R1 in ID (cycle 3) before I1 writes it in WB (cycle 5); forwarding from EX fixes it.

cse-2026-1-cs-7.approach: Solve the inner recurrence first with the Master theorem, then plug its order into the outer one. Comparing exponents $\log_b a$ with the driving term decides each case in one line.

steps.title: Solve $T_2$ first
steps.body:
For $T_2(n) = 5T_2(n/4) + \Theta(\log_2 n)$: $a=5$, $b=4$, so $n^{\log_b a} = n^{\log_4 5}$ with
$$\log_4 5 = \frac{\ln 5}{\ln 4} = \frac{1.609}{1.386} \approx 1.161.$$
The driving term $\log_2 n = O(n^{1.161-\varepsilon})$ (any $\varepsilon < 1.161$), so Master Case 1 gives
$$T_2(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_4 5}) \approx \Theta(n^{1.161}).$$

steps.title: Plug into $T_1$
steps.body:
Now $T_1(n) = 4T_1(n/2) + \Theta(n^{\log_4 5})$: $a=4$, $b=2$, so $n^{\log_2 4} = n^2$.
The driving term is $n^{1.161} = O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ with $\varepsilon = 2 - 1.161 = 0.839 > 0$ — polynomially smaller than $n^2$.

steps.title: Apply Case 1
steps.body: The leaves dominate: $T_1(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 4}) = \Theta(n^2)$ — option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: $f(n) = \Theta(n^{1.161})$ is polynomially below $n^{\log_2 4} = n^2$, so Master Case 1 gives $\Theta(n^2)$.
$n^2\log n$ would need Case 2, i.e. $f(n) = \Theta(n^2)$; but $f(n)$ is only $n^{1.161}$.
This is the order of $T_2$, not $T_1$ — it forgets that $T_1$ has its own $n^2$ recursion-tree leaves.
Adds a spurious $\log$ factor to $T_2$'s order (Case 2 mistake) and still ignores $T_1$'s own $n^2$ term.

cse-2026-1-cs-7.shortcut: $\log_4 5 < \log_4 16 = 2$, so whatever $T_2$ is (anything up to $n^{\log_4 5}\log n$), it is polynomially below $n^2$: $T_1 = \Theta(n^2)$ immediately.
pitfalls: Stopping after solving $T_2$ and picking (C).
Treating $\log_2 n$ as comparable to $n^{\log_4 5}$ and adding a $\log$ factor (Case 2) — Case 2 needs $f = \Theta(n^{\log_b a})$.
cse-2026-1-cs-7.verification: Recursion tree for $T_1$: level $i$ costs $4^i (n/2^i)^{1.161} = n^{1.161}\cdot 2^{0.839 i}$, a geometric series increasing towards the leaves, so the last level $4^{\log_2 n} = n^2$ dominates.

cse-2026-1-cs-8.approach: Check each statement against the TCP state machine: connection set-up is a three-way handshake, the connection is full-duplex, and either side may close — including both at once (simultaneous close).

steps.title: Set-up and duplex
steps.body: TCP opens with a **three-way** handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) — not two-way — so (A) is false. Once open, each direction has its own sequence numbers and data flows both ways at once: TCP is **full-duplex**, so (C) is false.

steps.title: Who may close
steps.body: Closing is per direction: either endpoint sends FIN when it has no more data. A server (e.g. an HTTP server closing an idle persistent connection) can perfectly well close first, so (B) is false.

steps.title: Simultaneous close
steps.body: If both applications close at the same time, both send FIN while in ESTABLISHED and go to FIN_WAIT_1. Each then receives the other's FIN, moves to **CLOSING**, sends an ACK, and on receiving the peer's ACK enters TIME_WAIT. The TCP state machine explicitly supports this **simultaneous close**, so (D) is true.

answer.value: The client and server **can initiate closing at the same time** — option (D)

optionAnalysis.reason: TCP uses a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN+ACK, ACK); two-way is not enough to agree on both initial sequence numbers.
Either side may send the first FIN; termination is symmetric.
TCP is full-duplex: both directions carry data simultaneously (and are closed independently — half-close).
Simultaneous close (both FINs cross; FIN_WAIT_1 → CLOSING → TIME_WAIT on both sides) is part of the TCP state machine.

cse-2026-1-cs-8.shortcut: Three facts: three-way open, full-duplex, symmetric close. Only (D) agrees with all three.
pitfalls: Mixing up "half-close" (one direction closed) with "half-duplex".
Assuming the client must close first because the client opened the connection.
cse-2026-1-cs-8.verification: RFC 793 Figure 14 shows exactly the simultaneous-close exchange drawn here; both sides end in TIME_WAIT.

cse-2026-1-cs-9.approach: HTTP 1.1 adds two things over 1.0: persistent connections (many request/response pairs on one TCP connection to one server) and pipelining (send the next request before the previous response arrives). Test each option against these, remembering a TCP connection has exactly two endpoints.

steps.title: Persistent connections
steps.body: HTTP 1.1 keeps the TCP connection open after a response (default `Connection: keep-alive`). The browser can then fetch the base page and all its objects — images, scripts — from that server over the **same** connection: (A) is true. Since persistence is per server, not per page, further **webpages** on the same server can also be fetched over that one connection: (D) is true.

steps.title: Different servers need different connections
steps.body: A TCP connection is identified by (client IP, client port, server IP, server port) — it joins the browser to **one** server. Objects stored on another server must be fetched over a separate connection to that server, so (B) is false.

steps.title: Pipelining
steps.body:
HTTP 1.1 allows **pipelining**: the client may send request 2 without waiting for response 1 to finish; the server answers in order. That is exactly (C), so (C) is true.

True statements: **A, C, D**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Persistent connections: all objects on the same server reuse one TCP connection.
A TCP connection ends at one server; objects on other servers need their own connections.
Pipelining: requests can be sent back-to-back without waiting for earlier responses.
Persistence is per server, so several pages on the same server can be fetched over one connection.

cse-2026-1-cs-9.shortcut: 1.1 = persistent + pipelined, both bounded by "same server". Anything crossing servers on one connection is false.
pitfalls: Reading (B) as true because HTTP 1.1 is "persistent" — persistence never spans servers.
Confusing pipelining (C) with HTTP/2 multiplexing; pipelining is already in HTTP 1.1.
cse-2026-1-cs-9.verification: Count RTTs for a page with 3 small objects on one server: non-persistent ≈ 2 + 3×2 RTT; persistent without pipelining ≈ 2 + 3 RTT; with pipelining ≈ 2 + 1 RTT — the savings come exactly from A and C.

cse-2026-1-cs-10.approach: $M e_2 = 0$ means the second column of $M$ is zero. From that one fact: the determinant is $0$, the rank is anything from $0$ to $n-1$, and the null space (a subspace) contains every multiple of $e_2$.

steps.title: Translate $Me_2 = 0$
steps.body: $Me_2$ picks out the second column of $M$, so the condition says **column 2 of $M$ is the zero vector**. Hence $M$ has a non-trivial null vector, i.e. $M$ is singular.

steps.title: Determinant
steps.body: A matrix with a zero column has $\det M = 0$ (expand along that column). So (B) is always true and (A), $\det M = 1$, is never true.

steps.title: Rank is not forced to be 1
steps.body: By rank–nullity, $\text{rank}(M) = n - \text{nullity} \le n-1$, but nothing fixes it to 1. Counter-examples: $M = I$ with its second column replaced by $0$ has rank $n-1$ (which is $\ge 2$ for $n \ge 3$), and the zero matrix has rank $0$ (for every $n$). So (C) is not always correct.

steps.title: Null space has many non-zero vectors
steps.body:
The null space is a subspace, so with $e_2$ it also contains $c\,e_2$ for every scalar $c$: e.g. $e_2$ and $2e_2$ (also $-e_2$) are distinct non-zero null vectors. Over $\mathbb{R}$ there are infinitely many, so (D) is always true.

Always correct: **B and D**.

optionAnalysis.reason: A non-zero null vector makes $M$ singular, so $\det M = 0 \ne 1$.
Column 2 of $M$ is zero (or: a non-trivial null vector exists), so $\det M = 0$.
Only $\text{rank} \le n-1$ follows; the zero matrix (rank 0) and $I$ with column 2 zeroed (rank $n-1$) are counter-examples.
The null space is closed under scaling: $e_2, 2e_2, -e_2, \dots$ are all non-zero null vectors.

cse-2026-1-cs-10.shortcut: One non-zero null vector ⇒ singular ⇒ det 0, and a line of null vectors ⇒ infinitely many. Rank is only bounded, never pinned.
pitfalls: Reading "rank $\le n-1$" as "rank $= 1$".
Forgetting that a null space is a subspace, so it contains all scalar multiples.
cse-2026-1-cs-10.verification: Take $n=3$, $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$: $Me_2=0$, $\det M=0$, rank $=2$, and $(0,c,0)$ is a null vector for every $c$ — B and D hold, A and C fail.

cse-2026-1-cs-11.approach: Use $X \oplus Y = X\bar Y$ when $Y$ implies $X$: here $\bar P Q \Rightarrow \bar P + Q$, so $F = (\bar P + Q)\cdot\overline{\bar P Q}$, which simplifies to XNOR. Then recognise which XOR forms equal XNOR.

steps.title: Simplify the XOR
steps.body:
Let $X = \bar P + Q$ and $Y = \bar P Q$. Whenever $Y = 1$ we have $\bar P = 1$, so $X = 1$: $Y \le X$. Then $X \oplus Y = X\bar Y + \bar X Y = X\bar Y$ (the term $\bar X Y$ is always 0).
$$F = (\bar P + Q)(P + \bar Q) = \bar P P + \bar P\bar Q + QP + Q\bar Q = \bar P\bar Q + PQ.$$
So $F = P \odot Q = \overline{P \oplus Q}$ (XNOR).

steps.title: Match the options
steps.body:
- (A) $\overline{P\oplus Q}$ is XNOR. ✓
- (B) $P \oplus Q$ is XOR, the complement of $F$. ✗
- (C) Complementing one input of an XOR complements the output: $\bar P \oplus Q = \overline{P \oplus Q}$. ✓
- (D) Complementing both inputs cancels: $\bar P \oplus \bar Q = P \oplus Q$. ✗

optionAnalysis.reason: $F = \bar P\bar Q + PQ$ is exactly XNOR $= \overline{P \oplus Q}$.
XOR is 1 when $P \ne Q$ — the opposite of $F$ (rows 01 and 10).
$\bar P \oplus Q = \bar P\bar Q + PQ$ (complementing one XOR input complements the output), which is $F$.
Inverting both inputs leaves XOR unchanged: $\bar P \oplus \bar Q = P \oplus Q \ne F$.

cse-2026-1-cs-11.shortcut: Evaluate F at P = Q = 0: F = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1. XOR-type options give 0 there (B and D); XNOR-type options give 1 (A and C).
pitfalls: Treating the overline in (A) as covering only $Q$ ($P \oplus \bar Q$ is also XNOR, so the answer is the same, but read the bar correctly).
Thinking $\bar P \oplus \bar Q$ is the complement of $P\oplus Q$ — two inversions cancel.
cse-2026-1-cs-11.verification: The four-row truth table (P, Q) = 00, 01, 10, 11 gives F = 1, 0, 0, 1, the same column as A and C and the complement of B and D.

cse-2026-1-cs-12.approach: Decode both numbers, compute each result as an ordinary integer, and check it against the sign-magnitude range of 8 bits, $-127$ to $+127$ (7-bit magnitude). Overflow is just "result out of range".

steps.title: Range
steps.body: With 1 sign bit and a 7-bit magnitude, representable values are $-(2^7-1)$ to $+(2^7-1)$, i.e. $-127$ to $+127$. ($-128$ is **not** representable in sign-magnitude, unlike two's complement.)

optionAnalysis.reason: $-52 - 76 = -128$: magnitude 128 needs 8 bits, but only 7 are available.
$52 - 76 = -24$, inside the range.

cse-2026-1-cs-12.shortcut: Opposite signs never overflow; overflow needs the operands to have the same effective sign. Only $X-Y$ and $-X+Y$ add magnitudes: $52+76 = 128 > 127$.
pitfalls: Using the two's-complement range: $-128$ is representable there, but not in sign-magnitude, so (B) is an overflow here.
Reading X as an unsigned number (180) instead of −52.
cse-2026-1-cs-12.verification: Magnitude check: $|X|+|Y| = 128 = 10000000_2$ needs 8 magnitude bits, one more than the 7 available — so both "same-sign" combinations overflow and both "opposite-sign" ones ($|76-52| = 24$) fit.

cse-2026-1-cs-13.approach: In a 1-indexed array heap, node $i$ has a child iff $2i \le n$. So internal nodes are $1..\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ and leaves are $\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1..n$. With $n$ odd, $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor = \frac{n-1}{2}$.
concepts: Array representation of a binary heap

steps.title: Leaf condition
steps.body:
Children of index $i$ are $2i$ and $2i+1$. Node $i$ is a **leaf** iff its left child does not exist: $2i > n \iff i > \frac{n}{2} \iff i \ge \lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1$.
For odd $n$: $\lfloor n/2\rfloor = \frac{n-1}{2}$, so internal nodes are $1, \dots, \frac{n-1}{2}$ and leaves are $\frac{n+1}{2}, \dots, n$.

steps.title: Indices that are leaves
steps.body:
- $\frac{n+1}{2}$: $2i = n+1 > n$ ⇒ no left child ⇒ leaf (the first leaf).
- $n$: the last element, $2n > n$ ⇒ leaf.

So options (A) and (D) **are** leaves.

steps.title: Indices that are internal nodes
steps.body:
- $\frac{n-1}{2}$: $2i = n-1 \le n$ ⇒ has children $n-1$ and $n$ ⇒ **not a leaf**.
- $\frac{n-3}{2}$: $2i = n-3 \le n$ ⇒ has children $n-3, n-2$ ⇒ **not a leaf**.

(For $n > 100$ both indices are valid, $\ge 49$.) These are the answers: (B) and (C).

answer.value: $\frac{n-1}{2}$ and $\frac{n-3}{2}$ are internal nodes — options **(B)** and **(C)**

optionAnalysis.reason: $2\cdot\frac{n+1}{2} = n+1 > n$: no child, so it is a leaf (the first one).
$2\cdot\frac{n-1}{2} = n-1 \le n$: children at $n-1$ and $n$; it is the last internal node.
$2\cdot\frac{n-3}{2} = n-3 \le n$: children at $n-3$ and $n-2$.
Index $n$ is the last node of the heap and has no children.

cse-2026-1-cs-13.shortcut: Last internal node = parent of the last node = $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor = \frac{n-1}{2}$; everything up to it is internal, everything after is a leaf.
pitfalls: Using $\frac{n}{2}$ as if $n$ were even and calling $\frac{n+1}{2}$ internal.
Treating the question as single-answer — two indices qualify.
cse-2026-1-cs-13.verification: Example $n = 11$ (same parity): internal nodes $1..5$, leaves $6..11$; $\frac{n-3}{2}=4$ and $\frac{n-1}{2}=5$ are internal, $\frac{n+1}{2}=6$ and $n=11$ are leaves.

cse-2026-1-cs-14.approach: Simulate the six insertions: compute $h(x) = (x+7) \bmod 11$, and on a collision probe $h, h+1, h+2, \dots$ (mod 11). Then read off which of the listed slots are still empty.

steps.title: Insert 11 — probes 7, 8, 9, 10
steps.body: $h(11) = 18 \bmod 11 = 7$: occupied (22). Probe 8: occupied (1). Probe 9: occupied (13). Probe 10: free ⇒ $P[10] = 11$.

steps.title: Insert 24 — probes 9, 10, 0, 1
steps.body: $h(24) = 31 \bmod 11 = 9$ ($31 = 2\cdot 11 + 9$): occupied. Probe 10: occupied (11). Probe $(10+1) \bmod 11 = 0$: occupied (15). Probe 1: free ⇒ $P[1] = 24$.

steps.title: Read off the empty slots
steps.body:
Occupied: 0, 1, 7, 8, 9, 10. Empty: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

Of the options, slot **0** (15), slot **10** (11) and slot **1** (24) are occupied; only slot **2** is empty — option (C).

optionAnalysis.reason: Holds 15, since h(15) = 22 mod 11 = 0 and slot 0 was free.
Holds 11: its home slot 7 and slots 8, 9 were taken, so it landed in 10.
No key hashes to 2 and no probe sequence reaches it (24 stops at 1), so it stays empty.
Holds 24: probing 9 → 10 → 0 wraps around and stops at the free slot 1.

cse-2026-1-cs-14.shortcut: Home slots 8, 9, 7, 0, 7, 9 form one cluster 7–10 that wraps into 0–1 — the six keys exactly fill 7, 8, 9, 10, 0, 1, leaving 2–6 empty.
pitfalls: Forgetting the wrap-around from slot 10 to slot 0 when placing 24 (then 0 or 1 is wrongly called empty).
Hashing with x mod 11 instead of (x + 7) mod 11.
cse-2026-1-cs-14.verification: Six keys occupy six distinct slots {0, 1, 7, 8, 9, 10}; 11 − 6 = 5 empty slots {2, 3, 4, 5, 6} — consistent, and only option C lies in that set.

cse-2026-1-cs-15.approach: Find two parse trees for a short string to prove ambiguity, then argue uniqueness for $abab$ by forcing each production choice. Decidability is immediate: every context-free language has a decidable membership problem (CYK).

steps.title: Two parse trees for $abb$
steps.body:
Since $abb$ starts with $a$, use $S \to aS_1bS_2$; then $S_1\,b\,S_2$ must derive $bb$:
1. $S_1 \Rightarrow \epsilon$, $S_2 \Rightarrow bS \Rightarrow b$: $\;a\,\epsilon\,b\,b$.
2. $S_1 \Rightarrow bS \Rightarrow b$, $S_2 \Rightarrow \epsilon$: $\;a\,b\,b\,\epsilon$.

Two different parse trees (shown) ⇒ two distinct leftmost (and rightmost) derivations of $abb$. So (B) is true and the grammar is **ambiguous**: (A) is true.

steps.title: $abab$ has a unique parse tree
steps.body:
It starts with $a$, so the root must use $S \to aS_1bS_2$ with $S_1\,b\,S_2 = bab$. Two splits are conceivable:
- $S_1 = \epsilon$, $S_2 = ab$;
- $S_1 = ba$, $S_2 = \epsilon$.

But $ba \notin L(S)$: a string starting with $b$ must use $S \to bS$, leaving $a$, and every $a$ is produced by $aSbS$, which also produces a later $b$ — so $a \notin L$. Hence only $S_1 = \epsilon$, $S_2 = ab$ (via $S_2 \to aSbS$ with both $S \to \epsilon$). One parse tree ⇒ exactly **one rightmost derivation**: (C) is true.

scene.title: Left: a parse tree of abb · Right: the only parse tree of abab

steps.title: Decidability
steps.body:
$L(S)$ is context-free, and membership in any CFL is decidable (convert to CNF and run CYK in $O(n^3)$). So the language is decidable and (D) is false.

True: **A, B, C**.

steps.title: Upper bound
steps.body: Subset construction: each DFA state is a set of NFA states, so there are at most $2^6 = 64$ DFA states (including the empty set as the dead state). Minimisation never increases the count, so the minimal DFA has **at most 64** states. Hence **65** and **128** are impossible.

steps.title: A 1-state DFA is possible
steps.body: An NFA (with 6 states, possibly redundant) accepting $\Sigma^*$ or $\emptyset$ has a **1-state** minimal DFA, so 1 is possible — the NFA need not be minimal, and nothing forces a lower bound above 1.

steps.title: Even 32 is reachable
steps.body:
$L_5 = \{w \in \{0,1\}^* : \text{the 5th symbol from the end is } 1\}$ has a 6-state NFA (guess the position, then count 4 more symbols) and its minimal DFA needs $2^5 = 32$ states (it must remember the last 5 symbols, all of which are distinguishable).

So 1 and 32 are possible; the values that **cannot** occur are **65** and **128**.
